tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Determine whether a continuous-time signal is periodic by verifying that some positive time shift T satisfies $x(t+T)=x(t) for every t$, connecting the result to later period, angular frequency, and harmonic analysis.

blocks.text: A periodic continuous-time signal repeats itself after a positive time shift. The cue is that the same waveform comes back at a later time, and the equality must hold for every $t$.
Check the definition on a simple repeating sinusoid. The point is to see one full cycle match the next cycle after a positive shift.

blocks.latex:
\begin{aligned}
x(t) &= \cos(2\pi t) \\
x(t+2) &= \cos(2\pi(t+2)) \\
&= \cos(2\pi t + 4\pi) \\
&= \cos(2\pi t) \\
&= x(t)
\end{aligned}

blocks.text: A signal can have more than one valid positive shift, so this lesson only needs existence of some $T>0$, not the smallest one. If no positive shift works for every $t$, the signal is not periodic; later lessons will use this idea for the fundamental period, angular frequency, and harmonics.

sections.section_title: Checking a Proposed Period from the Definition

example_content.example_prompt: Verify that $T=2$ is a period for $x(t)=\cos(2\pi t)$ by checking that $x(t+2)=x(t)$ for every $t$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a proposed positive shift. For $x(t)=\cos(2\pi t)$, test $T=2$ by substituting $t+2$ into the formula and checking whether the result matches the original signal for every $t$.
The substitution returns the original signal, so $T=2$ is a valid period. That is the definition in action: one positive shift works for every $t$.

sections.section_title: Finding a Valid Positive Shift for a Repeating Signal

example_content.example_prompt: A signal takes the value $1$ on $0 \le t < 1$, $0$ on $1 \le t < 2$, and $-1$ on $2 \le t < 3$, then repeats that three-part block forever. Find one positive $T$ such that $x(t+T)=x(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a repeating block description. Read one complete block, note that its length is $3$, and test that block length as the candidate positive shift.

The same sequence of values reappears after $3$ time units, and each subinterval in the next block matches the original block after that shift. Therefore $x(t+3)=x(t)$ for every $t$, so $T=3$ is a valid positive shift.

Show two identical cycles, with the first cycle spanning $0 \le t < 4$ and the second cycle spanning $4 \le t < 8$. Make the repeated landmarks easy to compare by including matching peaks, troughs, and endpoints, and add a visible horizontal bracket or arrow spanning one cycle length labeled $4$.

example_content.example_prompt: From the graph of $x(t)$, decide whether the waveform repeats after a positive shift and identify one visible shift that works.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the graph itself. Find one obvious landmark on a cycle, compare it with the same landmark on the next cycle, and read the horizontal distance as a candidate positive shift.
The same waveform shape reappears $4$ units later, so the landmark check matches the full cycle, not just one point. That gives one visible positive shift of $4$.
Because the whole graph matches after that shift, the signal is periodic. The graph is the cue, the repeated cycle is the rule, and $T=4$ is one visible positive shift.

sections.section_title: Showing a Signal Is Not Periodic

example_content.example_prompt: Show that $x(t)=t$ is not periodic by assuming a positive shift $T$ and checking whether $x(t+T)=x(t)$ can hold for every $t$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a monotone trend. Test periodicity by assuming a positive shift $T$ and substituting it into $x(t)=t$.
That forces $T=0$, which contradicts the requirement that a period be positive. So no positive $T$ satisfies $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for every $t$, and the signal is not periodic.

sections.section_title: Finding a Valid Positive Shift for a Repeating Signal

prompt_blocks.text: A signal takes the value $2$ on $0 \le t < 1$, $-1$ on $1 \le t < 3$, and $0$ on $3 \le t < 4$, then repeats that four-part block forever. Which positive $T$ makes $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for every $t$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The full repeating block has length $4$, so shifting by $4$ lines up every subinterval with the next copy of the block. The smaller shifts only line up part of the pattern, and $0$ or a negative shift do not satisfy the requirement for a positive period.

prompt_blocks.text: A signal takes the value $0$ on $0 \le t < 2$, $3$ on $2 \le t < 5$, and $-2$ on $5 \le t < 6$, then repeats that block forever. Which positive $T$ makes $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for every $t$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The full block length is $6$, so shifting by $6$ realigns the entire repeating pattern. The choices $2$ and $3$ only match individual subinterval widths, and $0$ or $-6$ are not valid positive shifts.

sections.section_title: Showing a Signal Is Not Periodic

prompt_blocks.text: Which argument correctly shows that $x(t)=2t$ is not periodic?

choice_blocks.text: Check only $t=0$; since $x(0)=x(T)$ for some $T$, the signal is periodic.
Because the slope is constant, the signal repeats after the shift $T=1$.
Assume a positive $T$ and compare $x(t+T)=2(t+T)$ with $x(t)=2t$; equality for every $t$ forces $T=0$, so no positive period exists.
Because the signal is linear, it is periodic whenever the shift is positive.
A negative shift such as $T=-1$ shows the signal is periodic in reverse time.

questions.correct_answer: Assume a positive $T$ and compare $x(t+T)=2(t+T)$ with $x(t)=2t$; equality for every $t$ forces $T=0$, so no positive period exists.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A period must work for every $t$, not just one time value. Substituting gives $x(t+T)=2t+2T$, and matching that to $2t$ for every $t$ forces $T=0$, which is impossible for a period.

prompt_blocks.text: Which argument correctly shows that $x(t)=e^{-t}$ is not periodic?

choice_blocks.text: Since $e^{-t}$ approaches $0$, it eventually repeats values and is periodic for a large enough $T$.
Check $x(0)=1$ and $x(1)=e^{-1}$; because those are different, the signal is not periodic.
Assume a positive $T$ and compare $x(t+T)=e^{-(t+T)}=e^{-T}e^{-t}$ with $x(t)=e^{-t}$; equality for every $t$ forces $e^{-T}=1$, so $T=0$, which is impossible.
Because exponentials have a constant ratio, the signal repeats after any shift.
A zero shift works because $x(t+0)=x(t)$, so the signal is periodic.

questions.correct_answer: Assume a positive $T$ and compare $x(t+T)=e^{-(t+T)}=e^{-T}e^{-t}$ with $x(t)=e^{-t}$; equality for every $t$ forces $e^{-T}=1$, so $T=0$, which is impossible.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A period must preserve the signal for all $t$. The shifted expression introduces a factor of $e^{-T}$, so matching the original signal for every $t$ forces $e^{-T}=1$, which means $T=0$ and contradicts the definition of a period.
